title: Playing the Fertility Game at Work: An Equilibrium Model of Peer Effects
venue: MPRA Paper No. 45914 (Munich Personal RePEc Archive); working paper, March 2013
design_class: structural/simulation (game-theoretic Nash-equilibrium peer-effects model with multiple equilibria, estimated via Ciliberto-Tamer partial-identification bounds; establishment/firm random effects for common shocks; sister-fertility exclusion restriction; individual Probit as reduced-form benchmark)
exposure: number (or share) of a woman's fertile-aged female coworkers at the same work establishment who have a child in the period (endogenous peer fertility)
outcome: probability of / number of women having a child (indicator for a birth between Dec 2002 and Nov 2005)
effect_estimate: Naive individual Probit: each additional coworker with a child raises own fertility propensity ~1.0 pp (basic), ~0.3 pp with individual controls, ~0.5 pp with contextual controls, positive and significant. Full structural model with firm/establishment random effects: sign REVERSES to negative average peer effects; turning on (homogeneous) peer effects yields a '5-percentage point decline' in the share predicted to have a child. Heterogeneous model: positive across worker types defined by age/education, but negative within age groups and among low-education women (who dominate the sample). Reported as parameter BOUNDS, not point estimates; equilibrium selection matters: two-type-by-education average peer combination changes fertility by +25 pp (highest-fertility equilibrium) vs -7.5 pp (lowest); ~40-50% of workplaces have multiple equilibria.
effect_se_or_ci: n/a — partially identified; 95% confidence parameter bounds reported in Tables 4/6/7 (not point estimates or SEs)
direction: mixed — negative average/homogeneous peer effect once common shocks are absorbed (more coworker childbearing LOWERS own childbearing), but positive within some subgroups and across types; net sign depends on model and equilibrium selection
identifies_diffusion_vs_common_shock: partial — the structural game plus firm/establishment random effects explicitly absorb workplace common shocks (naive positive effect flips to negative when they are added), and a sister-fertility exclusion restriction separates endogenous from contextual effects; but effects are only set-identified (bounds), residual peer self-selection/sorting into workplaces is only partly tested (public vs private sector), and the mechanism is a mix of economic (career competition, replacement/scale diseconomies) and social (conformity) channels
setting_sample: Denmark; merged administrative employer-employee + fertility register; fertile-aged women (20-40) working in medium establishments (10-50 employees) as of Nov 2002; 151,494 women across 31,725 establishments; birth outcomes 2003-2005
routing_check: confirmed A.3-adjacent (social-interaction/peer-effects evidence on fertility) but FLAG mechanism mismatch: the peer effect concerns the decision to HAVE a child among coworkers, driven substantially by economic channels (labor-market competition, leave/replacement costs) as much as social conformity — it is NOT specifically diffusion/social-learning of fertility CONTROL knowledge or acceptability. Borderline with A.3's core parameter; largest signal is workplace/career, not contraceptive diffusion.
risk_of_bias: n/a (theory/structural) for the modelling core; for its applied Danish estimates, ROBINS-I overall: moderate — strong design against common shocks and reflection, but only partial identification (bounds), possible residual sorting, and mixed/uninterpretable mechanism
notes: One of the two method/structural papers. It DOES deliver an applied fertility estimate (Danish register data), so it is not theory-only. Central methodological lesson relevant to A.3: naive peer-fertility correlations are positive but reverse to negative once workplace common shocks are absorbed — a clean illustration of the reflection/common-shock problem. Multiple equilibria and partial identification mean no single point estimate exists.
